what: Hungary parliament votes to remove president from office

clean_source_blocks.text: Since his party swept to power in April, Péter Magyar (left) has repeatedly called on Tamás Sulyok (right) to resign The Hungarian parliament has voted to remove President Tamás Sulyok from office, who was widely seen as a loyalist of former prime minister Viktor Orbán who lost power in April after 16 years. Prime Minister Péter Magyar's Tisza party used its two thirds majority to steamroll through the 17th amendment to the constitution, ending the term of Sulyok and the head of the Constitutional Court Péter Polt. It was the most dramatic day in parliament since the new government took office in early May, after its surprise landslide victory against Orbán's Fidesz party on 12 April. Sulyok now has five days to sign the amendment - his own political death warrant - or refer it to the Constitutional Court.

Hungary's parliament is set to vote on a constitutional amendment on Monday that could pave the way for the removal of President Tamás Sulyok, marking a significant step in Prime Minister Péter Magyar's efforts to reshape the country's political system following his election victory earlier this year. The proposed constitutional changes form part of a broader reform agenda launched by Magyar after his Tisza Party secured a two-thirds parliamentary majority in April on a platform promising sweeping institutional reforms following the 16-year rule of former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán. Magyar has repeatedly accused Sulyok and several senior state officials of remaining loyal to Orbán's political network, describing them as "puppets" of the former administration.
Tamás Sulyok was widely seen as a loyalist of former prime minister Viktor Orbán, who lost power in April after 16 years.

The prime minister has urged the 70-year-old president to resign voluntarily, arguing that he failed to defend democratic institutions and the rule of law during Orbán's tenure. According to the parliamentary schedule, lawmakers are expected to vote on the constitutional amendment at 6:15 p.m. local time, barring procedural delays. If approved, the legislation would provide the legal framework for Sulyok's removal. Should the president refuse to sign the amendment, Magyar has said his government would initiate impeachment proceedings in parliament. Although Hungary's president performs primarily ceremonial duties, the office retains the authority to return legislation to parliament or refer laws to the Constitutional Court for review. The proposed constitutional changes have generated debate both within Hungary and internationally. Orbán's Fidesz Party has criticized the reforms, describing the package as undemocratic and accusing the government of abusing its parliamentary supermajority.

Hungary's parliament is set to vote on a constitutional amendment on Monday that could pave the way for the removal of President Tamás Sulyok, marking a significant step in Prime Minister Péter Magyar's efforts to reshape the country's political system following his election victory earlier this year.

The proposed constitutional changes form part of a broader reform agenda launched by Magyar after his Tisza Party secured a two-thirds parliamentary majority in April on a platform promising sweeping institutional reforms following the 16-year rule of former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán.

If approved, the legislation would provide the legal framework for Sulyok's removal. Should the president refuse to sign the amendment, Magyar has said his government would initiate impeachment proceedings in parliament.

Although Hungary's president performs primarily ceremonial duties, the office retains the authority to return legislation to parliament or refer laws to the Constitutional Court for review.

The proposed constitutional changes have generated debate both within Hungary and internationally.

Orbán's Fidesz Party has criticized the reforms, describing the package as undemocratic and accusing the government of abusing its parliamentary supermajority.

Human rights organizations have also voiced concerns.

Amnesty International said President Sulyok should be afforded due process, while Human Rights Watch argued that the proposed constitutional changes resemble practices seen during the previous administration.

However, former Hungarian Supreme Court President András Baka defended the reforms, arguing that exceptional measures may be necessary to restore democratic institutions after years of political centralization.

Baka, whose own judicial mandate ended prematurely following legislative changes introduced under Orbán in 2011, said key state institutions had been structured to preserve the former government's influence even after an electoral defeat.

payload.title: Unkarin parlamentti hyväksyi presidentti Tamás Sulyokin syrjäyttämisen
payload.summary: Pääministeri Péter Magyarin Tisza-puolue käytti kahden kolmasosan enemmistöään perustuslain muuttamiseen. Muutos päättää presidentti Tamás Sulyokin ja perustuslakituomioistuimen johtajan Péter Poltin toimikaudet.
payload.content:
Unkarin parlamentti on hyväksynyt perustuslain muutoksen, joka päättää presidentti Tamás Sulyokin toimikauden. Pääministeri Péter Magyarin Tisza-puolue vei muutoksen läpi kahden kolmasosan enemmistöllään vain muutamia kuukausia sen jälkeen, kun puolue voitti Viktor Orbánin Fideszin 12. huhtikuuta järjestetyissä vaaleissa.

Muutos koskee kahta korkeaa viranhaltijaa

Perustuslain 17. muutos päättää sekä Sulyokin että perustuslakituomioistuimen johtajan Péter Poltin toimikauden. Kyseessä oli parlamentin dramaattisin päivä sen jälkeen, kun uusi hallitus aloitti työnsä toukokuun alussa. Tisza nousi valtaan yllätysvoitolla ja lupasi toteuttaa laajoja institutionaalisia uudistuksia Orbánin 16 vuotta kestäneen valtakauden jälkeen. Sulyokilla on viisi päivää aikaa allekirjoittaa muutos tai lähettää se perustuslakituomioistuimen arvioitavaksi. Magyar oli jo ennen äänestystä ilmoittanut, että hallitus käynnistäisi parlamentissa virkasyytemenettelyn, jos presidentti kieltäytyisi hyväksymästä muutosta. Perustuslain muuttaminen loi oikeudellisen perustan presidentin poistamiselle tehtävästään.

Magyar on vaatinut presidentin eroa

Magyar on toistuvasti kehottanut 70-vuotiasta Sulyokia eroamaan vapaaehtoisesti. Pääministerin mukaan presidentti ei puolustanut demokraattisia instituutioita eikä oikeusvaltioperiaatetta Orbánin kaudella. Sulyokia on pidetty laajalti entisen pääministerin liittolaisena. Magyar on kutsunut häntä ja eräitä muita korkeita viranhaltijoita Orbánin poliittiselle verkostolle uskollisiksi entisen hallinnon ”sätkynukeiksi”.

Presidentin tehtävä on pääosin seremoniallinen

Unkarin presidentin tehtävät ovat enimmäkseen seremoniallisia, mutta virkaan kuuluu myös lainsäädäntöön vaikuttavia valtuuksia. Presidentti voi palauttaa parlamentin hyväksymän lain uuteen käsittelyyn tai lähettää sen perustuslakituomioistuimelle tarkastettavaksi. Sulyokin ratkaisu määrää siten, eteneekö hänen oman toimikautensa päättävä muutos suoraan allekirjoitettavaksi vai tuomioistuimen arvioon. Orbánin Fidesz-puolue on arvostellut uudistuspakettia epädemokraattiseksi ja syyttänyt hallitusta parlamentaarisen määräenemmistön väärinkäytöstä. Muutokset ovat herättäneet keskustelua sekä Unkarissa että maan ulkopuolella. Hyväksytty muutos on keskeinen osa Magyarin uudistusohjelmaa, jolla uusi hallitus muokkaa valtion instituutioiden johtoa huhtikuun vallanvaihdoksen jälkeen.
summary_bullets: Parlamentti hyväksyi perustuslain muutoksen, joka päättää presidentti Tamás Sulyokin toimikauden.
Muutos koskee myös perustuslakituomioistuimen johtajaa Péter Poltia.
Sulyokilla on viisi päivää aikaa allekirjoittaa muutos tai lähettää se perustuslakituomioistuimen arvioitavaksi.
payload.journalist_note: Aiempi lähdeaineisto kuvasi tulevaa äänestystä, mutta myöhempi aineisto vahvistaa parlamentin hyväksyneen muutoksen. Sulyokin viisipäiväinen määräaika ja mahdollinen perustuslakituomioistuinkäsittely on huomioitu sanamuodoissa.

Since his party swept to power in April, Péter Magyar (left) has repeatedly called on Tamás Sulyok (right) to resign The Hungarian parliament has voted to remove President Tamás Sulyok from office, who was widely seen as a loyalist of former prime minister Viktor Orbán who lost power in April after 16 years. Prime Minister Péter Magyar's Tisza party used its two thirds majority to steamroll through the 17th amendment to the constitution, ending the term of Sulyok and the head of the Constitutional Court Péter Polt. It was the most dramatic day in parliament since the new government took office in early May, after its surprise landslide victory against Orbán's Fidesz party on 12 April. Sulyok now has five days to sign the amendment - his own political death warrant - or refer it to the Constitutional Court.

Hungary's parliament is set to vote on a constitutional amendment on Monday that could pave the way for the removal of President Tamás Sulyok, marking a significant step in Prime Minister Péter Magyar's efforts to reshape the country's political system following his election victory earlier this year. The proposed constitutional changes form part of a broader reform agenda launched by Magyar after his Tisza Party secured a two-thirds parliamentary majority in April on a platform promising sweeping institutional reforms following the 16-year rule of former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán. Magyar has repeatedly accused Sulyok and several senior state officials of remaining loyal to Orbán's political network, describing them as "puppets" of the former administration.

Tamás Sulyok was widely seen as a loyalist of former prime minister Viktor Orbán, who lost power in April after 16 years.

The prime minister has urged the 70-year-old president to resign voluntarily, arguing that he failed to defend democratic institutions and the rule of law during Orbán's tenure. According to the parliamentary schedule, lawmakers are expected to vote on the constitutional amendment at 6:15 p.m. local time, barring procedural delays. If approved, the legislation would provide the legal framework for Sulyok's removal. Should the president refuse to sign the amendment, Magyar has said his government would initiate impeachment proceedings in parliament. Although Hungary's president performs primarily ceremonial duties, the office retains the authority to return legislation to parliament or refer laws to the Constitutional Court for review. The proposed constitutional changes have generated debate both within Hungary and internationally. Orbán's Fidesz Party has criticized the reforms, describing the package as undemocratic and accusing the government of abusing its parliamentary supermajority.
